title: When reads outnumber writes: layers that take the load
dek: Most apps read far more than they write, and a database that copes with the writes can still sink under the reads. Here is how each layer, from the CDN to read replicas, takes its share, how to handle the one key everyone wants, and how to keep users from seeing their own changes vanish.

items: Most apps read far more than they write. A database that takes the writes easily can still sink under the reads.
Add layers that answer reads before they reach the database: the CDN, a cache, read replicas, and copies of data shaped for one screen.
Every layer serves slightly old data. Decide which reads must be fresh and send only those to the primary, and plan for the few hot keys every layer sees.

body.x: Count, and fix the cheap things first

Start with the numbers: reads a second at the peak, and how many of them repeat. A restaurant's menu is read thousands of times between changes; a customer's own order history is read by one person. The first is easy to cache; the second needs a good index and perhaps replicas.

Then fix what costs nothing: the right indexes, fewer queries per page (no query per item in a loop), and only the columns the screen shows. One missing index can cost more than every layer below can save.

body.cap: Each layer answers what it can and passes on the rest. Of 1 lakh reads a second, 400 reach the primary database.

body.x: When a page needs data from many tables, cache the finished answer instead of the pieces: one 'restaurant page' entry with the menu, rating and opening hours, rebuilt when any of them changes. Taken further, this becomes a separate read model. Writes go to the normalised tables, and a stream of changes keeps a denormalised copy, in a document store or a search index, that serves the reads. Splitting the write side from the read side like this is often called CQRS.

body.cap: A hot key turns one expired entry into a flood. Coalescing sends one request to the database, and a short copy in each server spreads the reads.

items: A hot key is one item read so often that the single cache node or row holding it is overloaded: the restaurant everyone orders from during a match, a celebrity's profile.
Coalesce: when many requests miss the same key at once, one fetches it and the rest wait for that answer. CDNs do the same and call it request collapsing.
Keep a copy of the hottest keys in each server's memory for a few seconds. They get slightly older; the cache node stops being the bottleneck.
Spread one key over copies: store menu:42 as menu:42#0 to menu:42#9 on different cache nodes, and read a random one.
Refresh hot keys a little before they expire, so they never expire under load.

body.x: A customer changes their address and the next screen shows the old one, because the read went to a replica 300 ms behind. Ways out:

items: Read from the primary for a short while after this user writes, say 10 seconds, or on the screens right after a change.
Remember the write's position in the database log and read from a replica only once it has caught up to it. PostgreSQL exposes this position as the LSN.
Delete the cache entry when the data changes, so the next read reloads it instead of serving the old copy.

body.x: 5,000 people a second open restaurant menus, 4 queries each, and no database in the Lab takes 20,000 queries a second. Put a cache in front and watch where the reads go.

body.label: Go deeper: why the hit rate matters more than it looks

body.x: At a 90% hit rate, 1 read in 10 reaches the database; at 99%, 1 in 100. Going from 90% to 99% sounds like a small gain, but it cuts database reads tenfold.

The danger runs the other way too. If a deploy or a full cache drops the hit rate from 99% to 90%, the database suddenly gets ten times its usual reads. Size the database for the hit rate on a bad day, and warm a fresh cache before sending it traffic.
